messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Colored Plots
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Colored Plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Eddie,

I´m afraid you are not thinking about this the right way. Remember that the physical dimensions of your data do not determine how variation is structured, at least not in the way you are suggesting. Of course for 3D data you have more data dimensions (3*k - 6 after superimposition), but how variation is structured across these dimensions, and what you see in a PCA plot depends on the particular characteristics of your sample, not on the physical dimensions of your landmarks. IN this respect, PCA works exactly the same way for 2D and 3D data, as it would for any kind of multivariate dataset.

I am not sure what you mean by "plots don´t seem correct", what criteria you are using for this judgement or what you are basing your initial intuition on, but PCA plots produced by plotTangentSpace give you the summary of your data. You can look at other PC dimensions (e.g. plot PC2 vs. PC3 or PC1 vs PC3) if you want, but it is not strictly necessary to plot the data in 3D (although you may want to do that to be able to visualize variation in more dimensions, no objection to that). 3D plots in R can be made (not surprisingly!) with the package plot3D.

Hope this helps, good luck with your plotting!
Antigoni

Hi Antigoni, Thank you for the reply.

I realized that perhaps the reason the plots didn't seem correct to me is because they were 2d plots. By trying to extract the scores of plotTangentSpace, I am essentially extracting scores of a 3d data set in shape space and was only using the x and y axes in my plot code above ($PC1, $PC2), which must have given me a plot that was not including the z axis. Is my intuition correct? This would make much more sense, and I presume that my next step would be to use a code in the plot3d package. If this is the case, which function in that package should I directly go to?

-Eddie

On Thu, May 31, 2018 at 8:33 PM Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Anderson,
>
> The nested.update function does not “deal” with imbalance issues.  It merely changes how F statistics are calculated in ANOVA.  I think the question you wish to ask is if despite your imbalance, does the least squares approach used with procD.lm provide reliable estimates?  You can consider this possibility by the following step by step process.
>
> 1. Turn your coordinates into PC scores for simplicity, e.g.,
>
> Y <- prcomp(two.d.array(geoall$coord))$x  # Assuming $coord is a 3D array
>
> 2. shape_lm<-procD.lm(Y~log(size)+ Temperature/Site,iter=9999,RRPP=T,data=geoall)
>
> 3. B <- shape_lm$coefficients; Yhat <- shape_lm$fitted
>
> 4. Run lmer, variable by variable, for the first few variables (Y[,1], Y[,2], Y[,3], …), e.g.,
>
> df <- data.frame(Y=Y, Temperature = geoall$Temperature, Site = geoall$Site)
>
> shape_lmer.1 <- lmer(Y[,1] ~ Temperature + (0 + Temperature | Site), data = df)
>
> 5. Compare fitted values from lmer to corresponding columns of Yhat, or coefficients to corresponding columns of B.
>
> If values are close, then you probably do not have to worry about biased LS estimates via procD.lm compared to the REML estimates in lmer.  If you are comfortable, then you could use nested.update for appropriate F values.
>
> Mike
>
> > On May 31, 2018, at 4:05 AM, Anderson Feijo <ande...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear all,
> >
> > I have been working with hierarchical models to explore size and other univariate terms using lmer4 package, which allow me to include as random factor localities with uneven numbers of observations.  Now I want to expand my study testing similar approaches using skull shape as dependent variable. I don´t want to reduce the shape dimension using PCA or regression scores of shape onto size to avoid miss any important information (as mentioned in this group several times). So, my question is, can nested.function deal with the uneven distribution of samples per locality issue?
> >
> > I run the code below and it seems to work fine. But after read previously related post in this group and the help function of nested.function I am not completely sure if it really can deal with this issue:
> >
> > >shape_lm<-procD.lm(coord~log(size)+ Temperature/Site,iter=9999,RRPP=T,data=geoall)
> > >shape_lm<-nested.update(shape_lm, ~Temperature/Site)
> >
> >
> > - Another question is that for the fixed factor alone I got a not significant correlation, but the interaction between Temperature:Site was significant. I am guessing that I should consider only the result of temperature isolated since I am interested in the general effect of temperature in my sample, is that guessing right?
> >

Dear all,

Please forgive me for posting another question here, but as it is related to the first answer I thought it might be easier to do so.
I'm afraid this is a bit of a basic question but I just want to make sure that I'm using a relevant approach.

I'm looking at skull shape in a sample of hominins, which means some of my groups have very few observations (the biggest has over 100 individuals, the smallest just 2, most have between 5 and 10). I have 6 species.
I ran a PCA to explore the data but I would like to assess the amount and significance of differences between groups and I thought the most relevant way to do this would be to compare group means. Can I run a MANOVA on this data and how can I check that I'm not violating essential assumptions? It seems to me that I'm trying to do pretty much the same thing as Russ in his first question so I tried out the code Mike suggested (advanced.procD.lm with coords ~ group, coords ~1, groups = ~group as models and group criterion), does that work in my case or am I missing something? Mostly I'm worried about those tiny samples.

Sorry again for the basic question and thank you for your help!

Lou

messages.body_plain:
Lou,

if I understand correctly your sampling scheme, you might not actually be able to run analyses like ANOVAs. To be able to compare means, you need to have a sample for each group based on which to calculate a mean and a variance (that´s why the analysis is called an analysis of variance). If any of your groups have n = 1, the functions will not work. Even if you have 2 or 3 specimens in each group (the numbers I am mentioning are just sequential, not intended to suggest a threshold), you should stop and think whether comparisons bare any real meaning. Maybe in your case, you should limit your inferences to visual inspection of your data, or addressing questions such as how shape varies across the evolutionary history of your clade, rather than trying to assess whether species are different or not, which is something you do not seem to have sufficient data for.

Hope this helps
Antigoni

Le vendredi 1 juin 2018 12:18:59 UTC+2, Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou a écrit :

> Lou,
>
> if I understand correctly your sampling scheme, you might not actually be able to run analyses like ANOVAs. To be able to compare means, you need to have a sample for each group based on which to calculate a mean and a variance (that´s why the analysis is called an analysis of variance). If any of your groups have n = 1, the functions will not work. Even if you have 2 or 3 specimens in each group (the numbers I am mentioning are just sequential, not intended to suggest a threshold), you should stop and think whether comparisons bare any real meaning. Maybe in your case, you should limit your inferences to visual inspection of your data, or addressing questions such as how shape varies across the evolutionary history of your clade, rather than trying to assess whether species are different or not, which is something you do not seem to have sufficient data for.
>
> Hope this helps
> Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
I believe I know what you are doing wrong.  The plot.advanced.procD.lm function is an S3 generic function.  What this means is that it can be used as a generic function, like plot, and the .advanced.proc.D.lm portion indicates to R what kind of class the object has, so it knows how to plot it.

If you are doing this:

plot.advanced.procD.lm(fit)

it will not work, but this will:

plot(fit)

I had not considered when I was trying to confirm if it works that one might type the entire function name.  When I just tried to do that, I got the same error you had.

I’ll re-iterate what Antigoni said before, that the advanced.procD.lm examples demonstrate this.  It might not be apparent, and it can be confusing because all functions must be listed in the index, but S3 generic functions never use the full name.  Whenever you see, e.g., print.procD.lm, summary.procD.lm, plot.procD.lm, you should realize that to make the functions work you use merely use print, summary, and plot, respectively.

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.subject: Partial least squares (shape coordinates v. latitude/longitude)
messages.subject_clean: Partial least squares (shape coordinates v. latitude/longitude)
messages.body_plain:
Hi geomorp-ers,

I posted earlier asking for advice about the covariance between shape data and geographical variables. I got some great suggestions (thanks to those who responded), but now I'm looking for some more specific advice--i.e., about running a partial least squares analysis.

I would like to examine the covariance between aligned shape coordinates and latitude and longitude using a partial least squares analysis (PLS). My question is whether or not I can examine how shape covaries with latitude and longitude in a single analysis or if I would need to do two separate PLS analyses (one looking at the covariance of shape and latitude and one looking at the covariance of shape and longitude). I would prefer the latter if possible, but, in that case, I'm not sure how to implement this analysis.

Any advice would be greatly appreciated, and I apologize in advance if this question demonstrates a fundamental lack of understanding of PLS (this is my first foray into this analysis).

Thanks,
Terry Ritzman

Hi geomorp-ers,

I posted earlier asking for advice about the covariance between shape data and geographical variables. I got some great suggestions (thanks to those who responded), but now I'm looking for some more specific advice--i.e., about running a partial least squares analysis.

I would like to examine the covariance between aligned shape coordinates and latitude and longitude using a partial least squares analysis (PLS). My question is whether or not I can examine how shape covaries with latitude and longitude in a single analysis or if I would need to do two separate PLS analyses (one looking at the covariance of shape and latitude and one looking at the covariance of shape and longitude). I would prefer the latter if possible, but, in that case, I'm not sure how to implement this analysis.

Any advice would be greatly appreciated, and I apologize in advance if this question demonstrates a fundamental lack of understanding of PLS (this is my first foray into this analysis).

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I did a Phylogenetic MANOVA to assess differences in beak shape between the groups means of a categorical behavioural category. I got slightly counter-intuitive results (at least for me). I got a statistically significant correlation between shape and UBF categories (meaning that there are significant differences between groups) but no significant differences between groups in shape, is this possible? Am I missing something?

Script:

beak_data <- geomorph.data.frame(coords = beak_coords2, diet2 = diet2, MA = ant.MA2, BM = log.BM2, UBF.C = UBF1, phy = birdTree)

PGLS.coords_UBF <- advanced.procD.lm(coords ~ UBF.C, coords ~ 1, group= ~UBF.C, phy = beak_data$phy, data = beak_data, iter=999)

summary(PGLS.coords_UBF)

summary:

ANOVA Table

           Df      RSS        SS     Rsq     F      Z Pr(>F)

Y ~ 1     174 0.059486

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am new to geomorph and I'm practicing the functions with the built-in "scallopPLY data set". I just encountered a problem of using the PlotTangentSpace function.

I first used the "buildtemplate" function to choose 9 fixed landmarks for generating 60 surface semilandmarks. I deliberately choose 9 different points on two same PLY scans of the scallop. I then use the "define.sliders" function to determine curve semilandmarks. After that, I use the "gpagen" function to perform the Procrustes analysis. So far so good at this step.

However, when I try to run a PCA analysis with the "PlotTangenSpace" function, R reported an error: "Error in dimnames(s$v) <- list(colnames(x), paste0("PC", j)) :
  length of 'dimnames' [2] not equal to array extent."

Could anybody tell what I did wrong?

I attached the created two ".nts" data sets ("data1" and "data2") generated by the "buildtemplate" function for two hypothetical scallops, as well as the .csv files of "curveslide" and "surfslide". Here are my codes:
setwd("..............")
filelist <- list.files(pattern=".nts")
data.coords<-readmulti.nts(filelist)
curvslide<- as.matrix(read.csv("curveslide.csv", header = TRUE))
surfslide <- as.matrix(read.csv("surfslide.csv", header = TRUE))
GPAtest <- gpagen(data.coords, curves = curvslide, surfaces=surfslide)
plotTangentSpace(GPAtest$coords) #("error at this step")

Thank you very much for taking your time to look at my question! I really appreciate your help!

Best regards,
Charles Zhang

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] A question about the function PlotTangentSpace
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] A question about the function PlotTangentSpace
messages.body_plain:
Charles,

That particular error occurs within the prcomp function, which plotTangentSpace uses to find principal components.  The prcomp function (and thus the R principal component analysis) is nothing more than a prescribed way of performing singular value decomposition (SVD) on either a covariance matrix or correlation matrix for data provided.  What is interesting about this error is that it occurs after the SVD has been performed when the function is attempting to label the axes.  There is a mismatch between the number of axes the function thinks there should be and the number the SVD produced.  The prcomp function assumes the data should be full-rank (unless one specifies otherwise).  I suspect your data after GPA might have some redundancies that caused the matrix to have a rank issue.

I think this could occur if your curves and surfaces designs are doing something strange.  I recommend trying a trial using a simpler version or curves and/or surfaces and see if the error persists.  If not, then maybe examine your original curves and surfaces matrices for errors.

If the error persists, then we will have to look into the issue further.

Good luck!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Convergence and divergence in allometry predicted values
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Convergence and divergence in allometry predicted values
messages.body_plain:
Andy,

The tests you referenced are specific tests based on estimates at small or large size, rather than least squares means, so no, geomorph does not have an option for tests like these, as it involves an arbitrary assessment fo where values should be estimated.  However, tools are available to help you construct your own tests.

I recommend you look into our new R package, RRPP, which can be installed with

devtools::install_github("mlcollyer/RRPP”)

(It can be installed via CRAN too, but we have added some new features on our github version.)  The lm.rrpp function will provide coefficients from many random permutations and the predict.lm.rrpp function allows one to make e.g., shape predictions at small and large sizes, over the same permutations.  With thousands of estimates of shape at small and large sizes - which you decide what small and large are - one can generate distributions of contrasts to test for convergence/divergence, the way the papers you cite performed such tests.  (There is also an option for plotting point-estimates with confidence ellipses.)

geomorph and RRPP are built on the same philosophy, but RRPP is more of bare-bones program for user-defined tests, with substantially more output for “downstream” analyses.  More about the package can be found here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/2041-210X.13029

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Charles,

I’m not sure if your problem was the same as the example you gave me that had only two specimens, but that did provoke a type of error we did not anticipate, as we did not anticipate somebody would do a PCA with only two specimens, this projecting data on a single line.  Nonetheless, this should be possible and I was able to generate the same error because it is as if we are asking R to label axes that we augment are impossible to exist.  The problem was in finding the correct tolerance.  We have an inherent mechanism to shave off redundant PC dimensions because of GPA.  With surface semilandmarks, the eigenvalues tend to decay toward 0 slowly in higher dimensions, so without augmentation, R does not know, for example, that 0.0000001 is effectively 0.  (The tolerance, if other than 0, will cut off these effectively redundant dimensions.)  We had a mechanism to find the tolerance and shave off extra dimensions, but the solution was not good if there was only one PC dimension.  (It made the tolerance 1, which meant 0 PCs.)

I added a catch to check if there is only 1 or 2 possible PCs and if so, not to adjust the tolerance.  Your example then worked for me.  I have made these change on github, so the package can be updated immediately..  Let me know if that solved the problem.  I suspect you might have something different going on with more than 2 specimens.

Cheers!
Mike

trajectory.analysis(f1=shape ~ chkpnt, traj.pts=3, data=gdf, iter=999, print.progress=T)

Error in La.svd(center.scale(x)$coords, 0, 1) :
  infinite or missing values in 'x'

gdf$chkpnt = factor(gdf$chkpnt)

[1] 191
dim(gdf$shape)
[1]  72   2 191

Does anyone know how can I fix this?

Thanks,

Avi

messages.subject: Am I in the right direction with this analysis?
messages.subject_clean: Am I in the right direction with this analysis?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Forgive me if this seems rather basic but I am new to geomorph package and geometric morphometrics in general. I have a dataset containing shape information for different populations of a species. I have been studying different posts in this group and trying to apply what I've seen to my dataset for the purpose of learning. Results make ecological sense but I want to be sure that I am doing this the right way.

So, I want to compare size (log(cSize)) and shape differences between different populations. Are the steps below in the right direction? Are there any missing steps, anything that I am doing wrong. I am also very keen on listening if you have any advice for further analyses.

1) GPA analysis with gpagen
2) Test log(cSize) for homogeneity of variance with levene test (not significant)
3) Examine log(cSize) histogram and test for normality with Shapiro-Wilk Test (significant, data is not normally distributed)
4) Kruskal-Wallis test for analysis of variance (significant)
5) Dunn test for pairwise differences.

Note: Below gives the same pairwise results. I am not sure which method is more appropriate.
advanced.procD.lm(f1 = log(size) ~ site, f2 = ~1, groups = ~site,  data = gdf)

6) Test for allometry
procD.lm(shape ~ log(size), data = gdf)

7) Homogeneity of slopes test (non significant, homogeneous slopes)
procD.allometry(f1 = shape ~ size, f2 = ~site * sex, logsz = TRUE,      iter = 9999, RRPP = TRUE, data = gdf)

8) Investigate shape ~ site while accounting the effect of size and get pairwise comparisons
advanced.procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ log(size) + site, f2 = ~log(size),  groups = ~site, slope = NULL, iter = 9999, data = gdf)

Thank you in advance,
Burak

messages.body_plain:
Burak,

You have interaction term Site * Gender, so your model for test of homogeneity of slopes would be:

procD.allometry(Shape ~ CS, ~ Site * Gender, ...).

For pairwise slope comparisons it depends on your research question, but considering Help documentation I think your model should be:

advanced.procD.lm(Shape ~ CS + Site * Gender,
                                            ~ CS * Site * Gender,
                                               groups = ~ Site * Gender, slope = ~CS, ...)

Best,
Milena

messages.body_plain:
Burak,

You mentioned two things in your thread, both related:

>
> Another side question: it seems that log transformed centroid size variables are not normally distributed in all of my different datasets. Is this normal? I've been reading the literature and nobody seems to have this.

> Examine log(cSize) histogram and test for normality with Shapiro-Wilk Test (significant, data is not normally distributed)

First of all, when considering assumptions for linear models, one should look at the normality of the residuals from the model, more so than the predictors.  There are many reasons why a predictor might not be normally distributed.  For example, imagine having multiple groups with different size ranges and most groups have small sizes but one group has large sizes.  A distribution of size would be skewed.

Second, normality is an assumption for residuals.  A Shapiro-Wilk test is an explicit test (which is easily rejected with large sample sizes) to test whether data conform to expectation if drawn from a normal distribution).  Rejection of the null hypothesis for this test is not the same as concluding that an assumption has been violated.  If a distribution of residuals is symmetric, a parametric test assuming a normal distribution of the error is probably robust despite very small departures from the assumption.

Third, I would not get too concerned about the normality assumption for residuals when using a non-parametric, resampling approach for generation probability distributions.  One of the reasons to use this approach is to not be constrained by such assumptions.  A gross departure from these assumptions might still be bad (especially the homoscedasticity assumption), but one can usually assess such things with the standard diagnostic residuals plots.  (There is no Shapiro-Wilk test for multivariate residuals, anyway).

Cheers!
Mike

There are many reasons why a predictor might not be normally distributed.  For example, imagine having multiple groups with different size ranges and most groups have small sizes but one group has large sizes.  A distribution of size would be skewed.
>
> Second, normality is an assumption for residuals.  A Shapiro-Wilk test is an explicit test (which is easily rejected with large sample sizes) to test whether data conform to expectation if drawn from a normal distribution).  Rejection of the null hypothesis for this test is not the same as concluding that an assumption has been violated.  If a distribution of residuals is symmetric, a parametric test assuming a normal distribution of the error is probably robust despite very small departures from the assumption.
>
> Third, I would not get too concerned about the normality assumption for residuals when using a non-parametric, resampling approach for generation probability distributions.  One of the reasons to use this approach is to not be constrained by such assumptions.  A gross departure from these assumptions might still be bad (especially the homoscedasticity assumption), but one can usually assess such things with the standard diagnostic residuals plots.  (There is no Shapiro-Wilk test for multivariate residuals, anyway).
>
> Cheers!
> Mike

Burak, Meilena,

Yes, this is correct, in general.  However, I would caution against using P-values as the sole indicator for how to plan pairwise comparisons.  The effect sizes are really small for all effects, together explaining about 11% of the shape variation.  The effect size is especially small for sexual dimorphism, so one could question is it is even worth considering.  Also, this analysis used type I SS, so order matters.  Maybe if sex was added first, then site, the meaning would change a little.  Regardless, the effects would still be small.

It would be just as appropriate, in my opinion, to decide to do no pairwise comparisons, as the variation is so small, anyway.

Best,
Mike

Thanks again to both of you for your helpfulness Milena and Michael,

I indeed did not pay attention to effect sizes and only focused on P-values. I will keep this in mind. But, please bear with me a bit more. Testing for shape differences with accounting for the difference in size doesn't yield a significant result. In this case I think I can say that shape difference between groups is caused by allometry. This brings me to Milena's answer. What is the reason for shape comparisons without adding size as a covariate at this point? Shouldn't I be investigating differences in size between groups?

And, lastly these are the results for pairwise comparisons for site with size as covariant, without size as a covariate and an lsmeans comparisons in centroid size. What is the most appropriate interpretation in this case?

Thankyou very much for your patience with me,
Best regards,
Burak

> Burak, Meilena,
>
> Yes, this is correct, in general.  However, I would caution against using P-values as the sole indicator for how to plan pairwise comparisons.  The effect sizes are really small for all effects, together explaining about 11% of the shape variation.  The effect size is especially small for sexual dimorphism, so one could question is it is even worth considering.  Also, this analysis used type I SS, so order matters.  Maybe if sex was added first, then site, the meaning would change a little.  Regardless, the effects would still be small.
>
> It would be just as appropriate, in my opinion, to decide to do no pairwise comparisons, as the variation is so small, anyway.
>
> Best,

> Mike

Thanks for the suggestions.
Looking at the dataframe, it looks like the problem is probably that the rownames might not match my phylogeny. For my previous analyses/manipulations, I had renamed the rows of the data (nose_shape2) to match the names in the phylogeny, but that doesn't seem to transfer in the geomorph dataframe.

Is there a way to change the row names in the geomorph data frame, or do I need to change the tip labels in my phylogeny? I get an error when I try to use the same commands for changing row names in a normal data set.

Thank you!

-Alyson

> Alyson,
>
>
>
> A few things to think about. First, be certain that the rownames for all components in the dataframe correspond with those of the phylogeny. Also, you did not specify the phylogeny in your procD.pgls, so that is an issue.

>

>
>
>
> data.cc <- sub_logdata[,c("INW", "ONW", "NL", "NW", "CL", "CW", "INW_Ratio", "NareWidth","Diet", "Avg_Mass", "For_Hab", "For_Mode", "Migr", "Echo_Mode", "FA")]
>
> data.cc <- data.cc[complete.cases(data.cc),]
>
> nose_shape2 <- data.cc[,1:8]
>
> ecovars <- data.cc[,9:15]
>
> df <- geomorph.data.frame(nose_shape2, ecovars, bat_tree)
>
> #Run PGLS
>
> procD.pgls(nose_shape2 ~ evovars, data=df, print.progress=F) #this is where I get the error
>
>
>
> I was using a tutorial and trying to translate it into my own data, so it is possible I've just missed a step or done an extra step? Trying to run a model with several morphological variables (nose_shape2) against a bunch of ecological variables (diet, habitat etc).
>
>
>
> Thanks for your help!
>
>
>
> -Alyson
>
>
>
>

>

> > Nadja,
> >
> >
> >
> > It could be one or a combination of changes made in our updates or R updates.  I don’t recall an explicit major change to geomorph data frames but it is possible an update somewhere else created an issue here, which we also neither tried to anticipate nor override. Geomorph data frames are R lists and the way you had it set up essentially asks R to try to give objects in the list a name or give up if it is unattainable. The solution I gave you is unambiguous because you define the names.
> >
> >
> >
> > Also, as a possibility, a change in the way our functions search the list to find data might have assumed that the list had names. I know that our old coding did not always do a good job to match names. Updated code has become more efficient. It might be that your example just happened to work better with our old code that had more bugs.
> >
> > These are speculative ideas. Invariably, with program coding, fixing one issue introduces another elsewhere.  I’m surprised your example worked with our old version. I would not have expected that. We probably just got lucky because we assumed the data frame would have named objects.
> >
> > Cheers!
> > Mike
> >
> >

> >

messages.subject: How can I correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population?
messages.subject_clean: How can I correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a question about correction of the data for the effect of different factors. I would like to correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population (exactly in the same way as in a pooled within group analysis in MorphoJ, in this case pooled within sex and population). I did a dummy regression of my shape data on dummy variable sex, and then I regressed the residuals of this analysis on the dummy variable population. However, Prof. Chris Klingenberg told me that this could only be done assuming that the two populations have the same patterns of covariation or that the populations differ the same way in both sexes. Also, the order of these regressions can slightly affect the results.

Therefore, I would like to do only one regression with two dummy variables (sex and population) in geomorph so that I can work with the residuals as shape data corrected for the effect of these two variables. Am I in the right direction with the interpretation of this analysis? How can I do this in geomorph? Thank you very much in advance!

All the best,

Nicole

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] How can I correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population?
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] How can I correct my shape data for the effect of sex and population?
messages.body_plain:
Nicole,

I believe the advice you were given is that you should explicitly test whether there is a sex * population interaction.  If there is, you should not try to “correct” your shape data, as sexual dimorphism manifests differently in the different populations.  You can do that with

procD.lm(shape ~ sex * population)

If the  sex * population effect in the ANOVA is significant, do not correct shapes.  If not, you can use the residuals from a new model

procD.lm(shape ~ sex + population)

which if added to the overall mean shape, will produce shapes that have held constant the effects of population and sex.  This is how I accomplish this:

newshape <- procD.lm(shape ~ sex + population, iter = 1)$residuals + procD.lm(shape ~ 1, iter = 1)$fitted

Keep in mind that you would also have to use arrayspecs to convert newshape back into an array rather than a matrix.

Again, the correction should be done IF, AND ONLY IF, you have determined there is not a meaningful interaction between sex and population.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Julie,

No, you do not need multiple columns for the variable, sex, when performing procD.lm.  To perform MANOVA to test for differences between sexes and to use procD.lm to do this are appropriate, but it sounds like you made a mistake when setting up the analysis.  To say it “does not work” with no details how it did not work makes it impossible to diagnose the problem.  However, likely issues could be with the format of your variable (sex), how you set up your model formula in procD.lm, missing data, whether you use a data frame in the set up, and possibly a mismatch in the number of specimens between the two data sets. The procD.lm help file should help resolve these issues.

I also recommend that next time you post an issue, you include your procD.lm coding, like you did for the gpagen, and the error message returned.  It will make it easier for someone to provide assistance.

Cheers!
Mike

Also, the order of these regressions can slightly affect the results.
> >

> >

Nonetheless, this should be possible and I was able to generate the same error because it is as if we are asking R to label axes that we augment are impossible to exist.  The problem was in finding the correct tolerance.  We have an inherent mechanism to shave off redundant PC dimensions because of GPA.  With surface semilandmarks, the eigenvalues tend to decay toward 0 slowly in higher dimensions, so without augmentation, R does not know, for example, that 0.0000001 is effectively 0.  (The tolerance, if other than 0, will cut off these effectively redundant dimensions.)  We had a mechanism to find the tolerance and shave off extra dimensions, but the solution was not good if there was only one PC dimension.  (It made the tolerance 1, which meant 0 PCs.)
> > >
> > > I added a catch to check if there is only 1 or 2 possible PCs and if so, not to adjust the tolerance.  Your example then worked for me. > > > > > That particular error occurs within the prcomp function, which plotTangentSpace uses to find principal components.  The prcomp function (and thus the R principal component analysis) is nothing more than a prescribed way of performing singular value decomposition (SVD) on either a covariance matrix or correlation matrix for data provided.  What is interesting about this error is that it occurs after the SVD has been performed when the function is attempting to label the axes.  There is a mismatch between the number of axes the function thinks there should be and the number the SVD produced.  The prcomp function assumes the data should be full-rank (unless one specifies otherwise).  I suspect your data after GPA might have some redundancies that caused the matrix to have a rank issue.

messages.subject: A question about whether geomorph can perform Bootstrap test with squared pairwise Procrustes distance
messages.subject_clean: A question about whether geomorph can perform Bootstrap test with squared pairwise Procrustes distance
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

May I ask a question about whether “geomorph” has functions for performing Bootstrap randomization test based on squared pairwise Procrustes distance? I apologize in advance that if my insufficient understanding of statistics and R might cause any confusions.

I plan to test the hypothesis that the dispersion of a small fossil group A i s not significantly larger than the dispersion (SSD) of an extant model taxon B. The dispersion is calculated by summed squared pairwise Procrustes distance (SSD) among all individuals of a group.

Basically, the idea is to calculate the SSD of the fossil group A as the test statistic, then using Bootstrap procedure to randomly resample model taxon B with the same sample size for many times (e.g., 10,000 times) to get a frequency distribution of SSD of each sample. Then I will compare the test statistic SSD with the frequency distribution of resampled SSD to see if it is significantly smaller. I also attached the paper that performed this test. The author used SAS to do the test.

I looked through the functions of the “geomorph” package, if my understanding is correct, it seems that Procrusted MANOVA can only test whether the sum of squared distance of some predetermined groups are significantly different from each other or not, rather than serving my purposes.

If “geomorph” does not have this function, could someone please give me some suggestions if there are any other package that can do this? I am thinking about perhaps export the test statistic SSD, as well as a matrix of resampled SSD, and do the statistical test with other package. Could any one give me any suggestions of how to achieve and export these data?

Thank you very much for taking time to read my question! If you need any other information, please do not hesitate to let me know.

Best regards,

Charles Zhang

Charles,

Geomorph does not do what you request automatically. However, this is simple to do in R, combined with geomorph. In R, bootstrapping is accomplished using ‘sample’, with replace=TRUE as an option.  One can simply write a loop where one bootstraps the data, performs whatever test one requires, and saves the output. Then, one evaluates over the set of bootstrap results for the desired test measure.
